# `async` and `defer` on `<script>`

## 1. Baseline: a plain `<script>` (no `async`, no `defer`)

When the HTML parser reaches a `<script>` element that has neither `async` nor `defer` (and is not `type="module"`), it **must stop parsing the HTML**, fetch the script if it has a `src` (synchronously, blocking further parsing until the fetch finishes), execute it immediately, and only then resume parsing the rest of the document. MDN calls this out explicitly: "Scripts without `async`, `defer` or `type="module"` attributes, as well as inline scripts without the `type="module"` attribute, are fetched and executed immediately before the browser continues to parse the page" (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/script). The WHATWG HTML Standard's script-element algorithm is the normative source for this "parser-blocking" behavior, and its attribute table defines `async` as "Execute script when available, without blocking while fetching" and `defer` as "Defer script execution" — i.e., both exist specifically to opt a script *out* of this default blocking model (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/scripting.html#the-script-element). javascript.info summarizes the practical effect: a blocking script "blocks" the page — nothing after it is visible until it has downloaded and run (https://javascript.info/script-async-defer).

## 2. `defer`

- **Parsing interaction:** The browser does **not** wait for a deferred script before continuing to parse HTML. The script is fetched in the background, in parallel with parsing, so it never blocks page rendering/parsing the way a plain script does (https://javascript.info/script-async-defer; https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/script).
- **When it executes:** Execution is held back until the HTML document has been fully parsed. Deferred scripts run "after the document has been parsed, but before firing `DOMContentLoaded`" (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/HTMLScriptElement/defer, cited via search snippet and corroborated at https://javascript.info/script-async-defer, which states "Scripts with `defer` always execute when the DOM is ready (but before `DOMContentLoaded` event)" and that the `DOMContentLoaded` handler itself "waits for the deferred script" — it only fires once all deferred scripts have downloaded and run).
- **Execution order with multiple scripts:** Deferred scripts are downloaded in parallel (whichever finishes first), but they are **guaranteed to execute in the order they appear in the document**, regardless of which one finished downloading first. javascript.info: "the `defer` attribute... ensures that the relative order is kept. So even though `small.js` loads first, it still waits and runs after `long.js` executes" (https://javascript.info/script-async-defer). The jakub-g gist states the same guarantee and notes it was historically buggy in IE9 and earlier (https://gist.github.com/jakub-g/385ee6b41085303a53ad92c7c8afd7a6).
- **`load` vs `DOMContentLoaded`:** Because deferred scripts must finish before `DOMContentLoaded` fires, they effectively "block" that event (https://gist.github.com/jakub-g/385ee6b41085303a53ad92c7c8afd7a6).

## 3. `async`

- **Parsing interaction:** Like `defer`, an async script is fetched in parallel with HTML parsing and does not block the parser while downloading (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/script; https://javascript.info/script-async-defer). However, once the script finishes downloading, it is executed **immediately**, which does pause the parser at that moment if parsing is still in progress (https://gist.github.com/jakub-g/385ee6b41085303a53ad92c7c8afd7a6: "doesn't wait for HTML parsing to finish; may interrupt DOM building").
- **When it executes:** As soon as it is available — there is no guaranteed relationship to `DOMContentLoaded`. javascript.info: "`DOMContentLoaded` and async scripts don't wait for each other," so `DOMContentLoaded` "may happen both before an async script... or after an async script" depending on which finishes first (https://javascript.info/script-async-defer). The jakub-g gist adds that async scripts do, however, block the window `load` event (but not `DOMContentLoaded`) (https://gist.github.com/jakub-g/385ee6b41085303a53ad92c7c8afd7a6).
- **Execution order with multiple scripts:** **No order is guaranteed.** Each async script is "completely independent" — other scripts don't wait for it and it doesn't wait for them; whichever finishes downloading first runs first (https://javascript.info/script-async-defer). The gist confirms: "relative order between `async` scripts execution is not guaranteed" (https://gist.github.com/jakub-g/385ee6b41085303a53ad92c7c8afd7a6).
- **Precedence rule:** Per the HTML spec's attribute description on MDN, "If the attribute is specified with the `defer` attribute, the element will act as if only the `async` attribute is specified" — i.e., `async` wins when both are present on a classic script (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/script). (This is mainly a legacy fallback pattern — `async defer` — for very old browsers that understood `defer` but not `async`, per https://gist.github.com/jakub-g/385ee6b41085303a53ad92c7c8afd7a6.)

## 4. Summary of order/DOMContentLoaded guarantees

| | Blocks parsing? | Executes relative to `DOMContentLoaded` | Order across multiple scripts |
|---|---|---|---|
| Plain `<script>` | Yes, blocks parsing until fetched+run | Before (parsing can't finish, so DOMContentLoaded can't fire, until it runs) | In document order (synchronous) |
| `defer` | No | After parsing completes, but **before** `DOMContentLoaded` fires | Guaranteed document order |
| `async` | No (but execution itself can interrupt parsing when it becomes ready) | No fixed relation — may fire before or after `DOMContentLoaded` | Not guaranteed — runs whenever it finishes downloading |

(Sources: https://javascript.info/script-async-defer; https://gist.github.com/jakub-g/385ee6b41085303a53ad92c7c8afd7a6; https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/script)

## 5. Inline scripts (no `src`)

For **classic** (non-module) scripts, `async` and `defer` only have meaning when there is a `src` to fetch. MDN's warning on the `async` attribute states it "must not be used if the `src` attribute is absent (i.e., for inline scripts) for classic scripts, in this case it would have no effect" (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/script). javascript.info states the parallel fact for `defer`: "The `defer` attribute is ignored if the `<script>` tag has no `src`" (https://javascript.info/script-async-defer). The jakub-g gist confirms both: "for inline (non-module) scripts, `defer` is ignored and has no effect (they are executed immediately)" and "for inline (non-module) scripts, `async` is ignored and has no effect" (https://gist.github.com/jakub-g/385ee6b41085303a53ad92c7c8afd7a6). So a classic inline script always runs synchronously at its position in the document, exactly like a plain script, no matter what attributes are set — this differs from module scripts (next section).

## 6. `type="module"` scripts differ from classic scripts

- **Deferred by default:** Module scripts are treated as deferred automatically, even without the `defer` attribute, and — unlike classic scripts — this deferred behavior **also applies to inline module scripts**, not just ones with `src`. The gist puts it directly: "`type=module` scripts... implies `defer`... for inline scripts, also implies `defer` (contrary to non-module scripts!)," and consequently there is a "guaranteed relative order of execution for all non-`async` module scripts (both inline and `src`)" (https://gist.github.com/jakub-g/385ee6b41085303a53ad92c7c8afd7a6). The dev.to walkthrough agrees: for module scripts "its loading mechanism [without any attribute]... is the same as the `defer` of the classic script," and explicitly notes that adding `defer` to a module script "has no effect. Because module scripts are 'defer' by default" (https://dev.to/zacharylee/html-script-element-attributes-async-vs-defer-vs-typemodule-5h6j).
- **`async` still works on modules, and behaves differently than on classic scripts in practice:** MDN's HTMLScriptElement `async` documentation states, "For module scripts, if the `async` property is set to true, the script and all their dependencies will be fetched in parallel to parsing and evaluated as soon as they are available" (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/HTMLScriptElement/async), and the same wording appears on the `<script>` element page (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/script). Because module scripts are deferred by default, adding `async` to a module script is what makes it run as soon as it (and its dependencies) are ready, out of order — the gist frames this nicely: "with legacy scripts, you generally use [async] to make things happen later, whereas with modules, you generally use it to make things happen earlier (this is because module scripts are deferred by default)" (https://gist.github.com/jakub-g/385ee6b41085303a53ad92c7c8afd7a6). Ordering for `async` module scripts is, as with classic `async`, not guaranteed relative to other async scripts (https://gist.github.com/jakub-g/385ee6b41085303a53ad92c7c8afd7a6).
- **Other module-specific differences** noted in the sources: module scripts execute only once even if the same URL is referenced by multiple `<script>` tags; they may `import` dependencies (part of why they need to be deferred); and fetches for module scripts (including their imports) are subject to CORS checks, unlike classic cross-origin script fetches (https://gist.github.com/jakub-g/385ee6b41085303a53ad92c7c8afd7a6; https://dev.to/zacharylee/html-script-element-attributes-async-vs-defer-vs-typemodule-5h6j). MDN's JavaScript Modules guide covers the broader module system (scoping, imports/exports, CORS requirement, execute-once semantics) though this research did not pull its full "Applying the module to your HTML" section text directly (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Guide/Modules).

## Sources consulted
- https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/script
- https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/HTMLScriptElement/async
- https://javascript.info/script-async-defer
- https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/scripting.html#the-script-element
- https://dev.to/zacharylee/html-script-element-attributes-async-vs-defer-vs-typemodule-5h6j
- https://gist.github.com/jakub-g/385ee6b41085303a53ad92c7c8afd7a6
- https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Guide/Modules (general module background only)

No disagreement was found among these sources on the core mechanics; they corroborate each other on parsing/blocking behavior, `DOMContentLoaded` timing, ordering guarantees, inline-script exceptions, and module defaults.
